questions.rationale: Reports should structurally distinguish confidence tiers (well-established vs. contested), not present all findings as equally authoritative.

questions.task_statement: Task 5.6 — Information Provenance and Uncertainty in Synthesis
questions.question: A synthesis report converts a set of financial figures into flowing narrative prose, rather than presenting them as a table. What issue does this raise?

options.A: None — prose is always the best format for all content types
options.B: Financial/tabular data often loses clarity and precision when force-converted to prose; format should match content type (tables for financial data, prose for narrative news, structured lists for technical findings)
options.C: This is required by the MCP resource specification
options.D: This can only be fixed using the Batches API

questions.rationale: Matching output format to content type (rather than uniform prose) is an explicit best practice for synthesis output design.

questions.question: A support session spans 30 turns. By the end, the agent both retains exact dollar figures (via a persistent case-facts block) and correctly declines to escalate despite mild customer frustration on an issue it's actively resolving. Which two Domain 5 techniques are being applied correctly here?

options.A: Stratified sampling and provenance tracking
options.B: The case-facts persistence pattern (5.1) and correct escalation-trigger judgment, i.e., not treating sentiment alone as an escalation signal (5.2)
options.C: Crash recovery manifests and `/compact`
options.D: Claim-source mapping and confidence calibration

questions.rationale: This scenario combines the two relevant task-statement techniques correctly: precise fact retention and appropriate (non-sentiment-driven) escalation judgment.

questions.question: A research pipeline experiences a subagent timeout mid-investigation. The coordinator receives structured error context, proceeds with partial results, and the final synthesis explicitly notes which sections have full source support versus coverage gaps. Which two Domain 5 task areas does this demonstrate together?

options.A: Error propagation (5.3) and provenance/coverage annotation (5.6)
options.B: Escalation resolution (5.2) and human review routing (5.5)
options.C: Context degradation handling (5.4) and case-facts persistence (5.1)
options.D: None of these areas apply here

questions.rationale: Structured error handling with partial-results continuation is 5.3; explicitly annotating coverage confidence in the final report is 5.6.

questions.question: A multi-phase codebase exploration uses scratchpad files, subagent delegation for specific questions, and inter-phase summarization. Midway through, the process crashes. What additional Domain 5 mechanism would best support recovery?

options.A: A structured state manifest that the coordinator can load on resume and inject into agent prompts
options.B: Simply restarting from scratch with no memory of prior work
options.C: Switching immediately to the Batches API
options.D: Disabling all subagents going forward

questions.rationale: Manifest-based crash recovery is the specific mechanism designed for exactly this situation, complementing (but distinct from) the other context-management techniques already in use.

questions.question: A pipeline uses field-level confidence scores calibrated against a labeled set, routes low-confidence and ambiguous-source cases to human review, and validates accuracy broken down by document type. What Domain 5 principle unifies all three practices?

options.A: Provenance preservation
options.B: Rigorous, evidence-based human-review workflow design that doesn't over-trust aggregate metrics or raw uncalibrated model outputs
options.C: Error propagation across multi-agent systems
options.D: Context window management

questions.rationale: All three practices are facets of Task 5.5's core theme: don't trust surface-level signals (aggregate accuracy, raw confidence) without validation.

questions.question: A support agent correctly (a) asks for an additional identifier when multiple customer records match, and (b) escalates immediately when a customer explicitly requests a human, without first investigating. What do both behaviors have in common from a Domain 5 perspective?

options.A: Both are examples of provenance tracking
options.B: Both reflect correctly recognizing specific, well-defined triggers (ambiguous match, explicit request) rather than defaulting to a guess or a blanket policy
options.C: Both require the Batches API
options.D: Both are unrelated to escalation/ambiguity resolution

questions.rationale: Both are concrete applications of Task 5.2's principle: respond to specific, legitimate triggers rather than heuristics or blanket rules.

questions.question: Which combination of failures would be worst for a research pipeline's reliability, combining two separate Domain 5 anti-patterns?

options.A: A subagent silently suppresses a real failure as a success (5.3), and the final synthesis presents the resulting incomplete findings as fully comprehensive with no coverage annotation (5.6)
options.B: A subagent correctly retries a transient error, and the synthesis correctly annotates a coverage gap
options.C: A subagent escalates a policy gap, and the coordinator asks for a customer identifier
options.D: The coordinator uses `/compact` and a scratchpad file

questions.rationale: This combines two named anti-patterns (silent suppression, and failing to annotate coverage gaps) compounding into a report that appears complete but is actually silently incomplete and unflagged.

questions.question: A developer resumes a named session after two days without mentioning that three files were modified externally in the meantime. The agent proceeds to make changes based on its stale understanding of those files. Which Domain 5 (and cross-domain, Task 1.7) principle was violated?

options.A: Provenance preservation
options.B: The requirement to explicitly inform a resumed session about file changes, since it won't automatically detect them
options.C: Stratified sampling
options.D: The `/memory` command's function

questions.rationale: This is a direct real-world consequence of not following the resume-with-file-change-notification pattern (Task 1.7, closely tied to Domain 5's context-currency concerns).

questions.question: A batch of documents is processed with confidence scores, but the scores were never validated against any labeled data — they're used as-is straight from the model. Six months later, an audit reveals the "high-confidence" bucket actually had a 15% error rate. What was skipped?

options.A: Nothing was skipped; this is expected variance
options.B: Calibration of confidence scores against a labeled validation set, which would have revealed the miscalibration before it caused six months of under-reviewed errors
options.C: The Batches API's built-in calibration feature
options.D: `tool_choice: "any"` configuration

questions.rationale: This is a real-world consequence of skipping the calibration step described in Task 5.5 — trusting raw scores led to a hidden, costly error rate.

questions.question: A report states a statistic with no source, no date, and doesn't indicate whether it's well-established or preliminary. A reader has no way to assess its reliability. Which three Domain 5.6 practices, if all had been followed, would have prevented this?

options.A: Claim-source mapping preservation, requiring publication dates, and structuring reports to distinguish confidence tiers
options.B: Case-facts persistence, scratchpad files, and `/compact`
options.C: Escalation criteria, stratified sampling, and manifest-based recovery
options.D: None of these practices are relevant to this problem

questions.rationale: All three named 5.6 practices, working together, directly address exactly this failure: unsourced, undated, unqualified claims.

questions.question: A 25-turn support conversation reaches a point where the agent needs to recall the exact order number mentioned in turn 2. Assuming no case-facts block was used, what's the most likely outcome, and why?

options.A: Perfect recall, since models never lose track of details in long conversations
options.B: A risk of imprecise or lost recall, since the detail may have been compressed away during progressive summarization and is deep in the "middle" of a long conversation, away from the more reliably attended beginning/end
options.C: The conversation would fail to continue entirely
options.D: The order number would automatically be moved to a separate database

questions.rationale: Without the case-facts persistence pattern, this scenario combines both named Task 5.1 risks: summarization erosion and lost-in-the-middle positioning.

questions.question: A coordinator's error-handling code distinguishes between `errorCategory: "transient"` (retry locally) and structural failures needing escalation, and separately, its synthesis step distinguishes well-supported findings from contested ones. Which two domains' principles are both being applied here, and how do they relate?

options.A: Domain 2 (structured MCP errors) and Domain 5 (provenance/confidence-tier reporting) — both rely on structured metadata to enable better downstream decisions, one for errors, one for findings
options.B: Domain 3 and Domain 4 only
options.C: This only reflects Domain 1 principles
options.D: These two practices are unrelated

questions.rationale: This question tests recognizing a shared underlying pattern (structured metadata enabling better downstream decisions) across two different domains and use cases.

questions.question: Which best distinguishes Task 5.5 (human review workflows) from Task 4.4 (validation/retry loops), given both deal with handling extraction problems?

options.A: They are identical and redundant
options.B: 4.4 is about automatically correcting recoverable extraction failures via retry; 5.5 is about routing genuinely uncertain or low-confidence cases to human judgment when automated correction isn't appropriate or sufficient
options.C: 5.5 only applies to batch processing; 4.4 only applies to real-time processing
options.D: 4.4 requires human involvement; 5.5 does not

questions.rationale: This distinguishes two complementary but distinct reliability mechanisms: automated self-correction (4.4) versus human-in-the-loop routing for genuine uncertainty (5.5).

questions.question: A coordinator receives partial results after a subagent failure, with structured context on what was attempted. It decides to proceed with synthesis rather than retry, since the missing information isn't critical to the report's core conclusions. Is this decision consistent with Domain 5 principles?

options.A: No — the coordinator must always retry regardless of context
options.B: Yes — this is exactly the kind of intelligent recovery decision that structured error context (rather than a generic failure message) is designed to enable
options.C: No — the coordinator must always terminate the workflow on any subagent failure
options.D: This decision is irrelevant to Domain 5

questions.rationale: This demonstrates the coordinator using structured error context correctly to make a judgment call, rather than defaulting to either blind retry or full termination.

questions.question: A support agent's tool outputs are trimmed to relevant fields, its case facts persist across turns, and its escalation logic uses explicit criteria rather than sentiment. Which Domain 5 tasks does this combination draw from?

options.A: 5.1 (context preservation) and 5.2 (escalation) only
options.C: 5.6 only
options.D: None — this combination isn't coherent

questions.rationale: This correctly identifies that trimmed tool outputs and case-facts persistence are 5.1, while explicit non-sentiment-based escalation criteria are 5.2.

questions.question: A team's crash-recovery manifest includes each agent's completed steps and key findings but omits any note about which files were still being actively modified at the time of the crash. What risk does this omission create?

options.A: None — the manifest is already sufficient for full recovery
options.B: On resume, the coordinator may not know which files require re-verification for consistency with in-progress changes at the time of the crash, risking incorrect assumptions about file state
options.C: This can only be resolved by discarding the manifest entirely
options.D: This is unrelated to the manifest's purpose

questions.rationale: This extends the manifest concept to a realistic gap: manifests need to capture enough state detail to support genuinely safe resumption, not just high-level progress.

questions.question: A pipeline correctly implements nullable fields (Domain 4) to avoid fabrication, and separately implements stratified sampling by document type (Domain 5) to catch accuracy issues. How do these two techniques complement each other?

options.A: They don't relate to each other at all
options.B: Nullable fields reduce one source of extraction error (fabrication under forced-required fields); stratified sampling helps detect remaining accuracy issues (including ones nullable fields alone wouldn't prevent) across specific segments
options.C: Nullable fields make stratified sampling unnecessary
options.D: Stratified sampling makes nullable fields unnecessary

questions.rationale: This tests recognizing that these are complementary, not redundant, reliability techniques addressing different failure modes at different pipeline stages.

questions.question: Overall, which best captures Domain 5's central theme across all six task statements?

options.A: Reliability is achieved primarily by using bigger models with larger context windows
options.B: Reliability comes from actively managing what information survives across context boundaries, applying well-defined (not proxy-based) triggers for escalation and review, structuring errors and findings with enough metadata for good downstream decisions, and never over-trusting aggregate or self-reported signals without validation
options.C: Reliability only matters for customer-facing agents, not internal research or coding tools
options.D: Domain 5 is primarily about reducing API costs

questions.rationale: This synthesizes the domain's throughline across preservation, escalation, error propagation, codebase context, human review, and provenance: deliberate information management and validated, non-proxy signals drive reliability.

questions.question: A coordinator's loop checks whether Claude's response contains conversational phrases like "I have finished researching" to decide whether to stop invoking tools. What is the correct, reliable replacement for this check?

options.A: Check the `stop_reason` field: continue on "tool_use", terminate on "end_turn"
options.B: Add more phrase variants to the keyword list to catch edge cases
options.C: Ask Claude to output a special JSON flag `{"done": true}` in its text and parse that instead
options.D: Cap the loop at a fixed number of iterations and stop regardless of content

questions.rationale: `stop_reason` is the structured signal the API provides specifically for this purpose. Natural-language parsing (B, C) is inherently unreliable regardless of the exact keyword or format chosen, and a fixed iteration cap (D) doesn't reflect whether the task actually finished.

questions.question: When `stop_reason` is `"tool_use"`, what must happen before the next request is sent to Claude?

options.A: The requested tool must be executed and its result appended to the conversation history
options.B: The conversation should be summarized before continuing
options.C: The loop should pause and wait for human confirmation on every call
options.D: The system prompt should be regenerated with updated instructions

questions.rationale: The agentic loop's core mechanism is: execute the requested tool, then feed the result back into conversation history so Claude can reason about the next action.

questions.question: In a hub-and-spoke multi-agent architecture, which statement is accurate?

options.A: Subagents communicate directly with each other to save latency
options.B: The coordinator routes all inter-subagent communication, error handling, and information flow
options.C: Each subagent independently decides which other subagents to invoke
options.D: The coordinator only aggregates final results and has no role in task decomposition

questions.rationale: Hub-and-spoke means the coordinator is the single point managing communication and routing between subagents, which supports observability and consistent error handling — direct subagent-to-subagent communication (A) defeats this pattern.

questions.question: A coordinator invokes all four available subagents (search, analysis, synthesis, citation-check) on every query regardless of complexity, even for simple factual lookups. What's the main downside of this design?

options.A: It reduces the risk of incomplete research coverage
options.B: It adds unnecessary latency and cost for queries that didn't need the full pipeline
options.C: It violates the hub-and-spoke pattern
options.D: It prevents parallel subagent execution

questions.rationale: A well-designed coordinator dynamically selects which subagents to invoke based on query complexity rather than always routing through the full pipeline — always invoking everything wastes latency and cost on simple queries.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.3 — Subagent Invocation, Context Passing, and Spawning
questions.question: What must be true of a coordinator agent's configuration for it to be able to spawn subagents at all?

options.A: Its `allowedTools` list must include "Task"
options.B: It must have a `context: fork` setting in its own definition
options.C: It must be running in plan mode
options.D: It must be invoked via a custom slash command

questions.rationale: The Task tool is the mechanism for spawning subagents, and the coordinator's `allowedTools` must explicitly include "Task" for this to be available.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.3 — Subagent Invocation, Context Passing, and Spawning
questions.question: A synthesis subagent produces vague, generic conclusions instead of using the specific findings from the web-search and document-analysis subagents. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: The synthesis subagent's model is not capable enough for the task
options.B: The coordinator did not explicitly include the prior agents' findings in the synthesis subagent's prompt
options.C: The subagents should have been run sequentially instead of in parallel
options.D: The Task tool has a hidden limit on how much context it can pass

questions.rationale: Subagents do not automatically inherit the coordinator's or other subagents' conversation history — findings must be explicitly included in the prompt when spawning the subagent, or it has nothing concrete to synthesize from.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.3 — Subagent Invocation, Context Passing, and Spawning
questions.question: You want two subagents to run concurrently rather than one after another. How should the coordinator's response be structured to achieve this?

options.A: Emit both Task tool calls within a single coordinator response
options.B: Emit one Task call, wait for its result, then emit the second in a following turn
options.C: Use `fork_session` to duplicate the coordinator's context for each subagent
options.D: Set `tool_choice: "any"` on the coordinator

questions.rationale: Parallel subagent execution is achieved by emitting multiple Task tool calls within a single coordinator response, rather than issuing them across separate sequential turns.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.4 — Multi-Step Workflow Enforcement and Handoff
questions.question: A refund workflow must never execute unless customer identity has already been verified. Which approach guarantees this ordering?

options.A: A system prompt instruction stating verification must happen first
options.B: A programmatic prerequisite gate that blocks the refund tool until the verification tool has returned a confirmed result
options.C: Few-shot examples demonstrating the correct order
options.D: A reminder appended to each user turn about the required order

questions.rationale: Prompt-based guidance (A, C, D) is probabilistic and has a non-zero failure rate. Only a programmatic gate — blocking the dependent tool call until the prerequisite has actually completed — gives a deterministic guarantee, which matters when consequences (like an unverified refund) are financial.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.4 — Multi-Step Workflow Enforcement and Handoff
questions.question: When an agent escalates a complex case mid-conversation to a human who has no access to the chat transcript, what should the handoff include?

options.A: Just the customer's original message, verbatim
options.B: A structured summary with customer details, root cause analysis, and recommended next action
options.C: The full raw tool call history with no synthesis
options.D: Nothing — the human agent should re-investigate from scratch for accuracy

questions.rationale: Since the receiving human has no transcript access, a structured handoff summary (customer details, root cause, recommended action) is what allows them to act quickly without re-doing the investigation.

questions.question: Different MCP tools return dates in inconsistent formats (Unix timestamps, ISO 8601 strings, etc.), causing the agent to misinterpret ordering. What's the best fix?

options.A: Add a `PostToolUse` hook that normalizes all date formats before the agent processes tool results
options.B: Instruct the agent in the system prompt to convert dates itself before reasoning
options.C: Add few-shot examples showing correctly ordered dates
options.D: Ask each MCP server owner to agree on a shared date format over time

questions.rationale: A `PostToolUse` hook can deterministically normalize heterogeneous data formats before the model ever sees them, which is more reliable than hoping the model correctly interprets and converts inconsistent formats itself.

questions.question: You want to guarantee that refunds above $500 are never processed automatically, no matter what the model decides. What's the most reliable mechanism?

options.A: A system prompt rule stating refunds above $500 require escalation
options.B: A hook that intercepts the outgoing `process_refund` tool call and blocks it above the threshold, redirecting to escalation
options.C: A few-shot example showing a refund being escalated at $600
options.D: Trusting the agent's self-reported confidence score before allowing large refunds

questions.rationale: Hooks intercepting outgoing tool calls provide deterministic enforcement of business rules. Prompt-based rules (A, C) and self-reported confidence (D) are all probabilistic and insufficient when a hard guarantee is required.

questions.question: A code review needs to check each of 14 changed files for local issues, then separately check for issues that only appear when files interact. Which decomposition pattern fits best?

options.A: A single pass reading all 14 files together
options.B: Prompt chaining: a per-file analysis pass, followed by a separate cross-file integration pass
options.C: One dynamic, adaptively-generated subtask per file discovered at runtime
options.D: A single subagent given all 14 files and unlimited time

questions.rationale: This is a predictable, multi-aspect review — well suited to prompt chaining (fixed sequential steps: per-file pass, then integration pass) rather than dynamic decomposition, which is better suited to open-ended, less predictable investigation tasks.

questions.question: You're asked to "add comprehensive tests to a legacy codebase" with no further detail. What decomposition approach is most appropriate?

options.A: A fixed prompt chain with the same steps regardless of what's discovered
options.B: Dynamic decomposition: first map the codebase structure, identify high-impact areas, then build a prioritized plan that adapts as dependencies are discovered
options.C: Immediately generate tests for every file in alphabetical order
options.D: Ask a single subagent to write all tests in one pass with no exploration step

questions.rationale: Open-ended, under-specified tasks benefit from dynamic decomposition, where subtasks are generated based on what's discovered during exploration, rather than a fixed pipeline decided upfront.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.7 — Session State, Resumption, and Forking
questions.question: You want to explore two different refactoring approaches starting from the same point in an analysis, without either exploration affecting the other. What should you use?

options.A: `--resume` with the same session name for both explorations
options.B: `fork_session` to create two independent branches from the shared baseline
options.C: Start two completely fresh sessions with no shared context
options.D: Use `/compact` twice to create two condensed copies

questions.rationale: `fork_session` is designed exactly for this: creating independent branches from a shared analysis baseline so divergent approaches can be explored without interfering with each other.

questions.task_statement: Task 1.7 — Session State, Resumption, and Forking
questions.question: You resume a named session to continue investigating a codebase, but several files have since been modified by teammates. What should you do?

options.A: Trust the resumed session's prior tool results without changes, since resumption preserves everything needed
options.B: Inform the agent about the specific file changes so it can perform targeted re-analysis
options.C: Start an entirely new session and re-explore the whole codebase from scratch every time
options.D: Use `fork_session` instead, since it automatically detects file changes

questions.rationale: Resumed sessions can hold stale tool results. Explicitly informing the agent about specific changes enables targeted re-analysis, which is more reliable than assuming old results are still valid or over-correcting with a full re-exploration.

questions.question: A research coordinator produces a synthesis with confident, unified conclusions even though two of its subagents reported partial failures (one search timed out, one document was inaccessible). What's the most likely design flaw?

options.A: The synthesis subagent is not capable enough for the task
options.B: Subagent errors were suppressed or not propagated with enough context for the coordinator to annotate coverage gaps
options.C: The system should have used a single agent instead of multiple
options.D: The web search subagent needs a larger context window

questions.rationale: When partial failures occur, structured error propagation should let the coordinator annotate the final synthesis with coverage gaps rather than presenting an artificially confident, complete-looking result.

questions.question: A customer's message raises three unrelated issues at once (a billing question, a shipping delay, and a product defect). What's the best way for the agent to handle this?

options.A: Only address the first issue mentioned and ask the customer to submit separate requests for the rest
options.B: Decompose the message into distinct items, investigate each using shared context, then synthesize a single unified resolution
options.C: Escalate immediately since multi-issue messages are inherently too complex
options.D: Pick the issue that seems most urgent and ignore the others

questions.rationale: Multi-concern requests should be decomposed into distinct items and investigated in parallel using shared context, then synthesized into one coherent response — not dropped, escalated by default, or handled one at a time in isolation.

questions.question: Which of the following is an anti-pattern for determining when an agentic loop should stop?

options.A: Checking `stop_reason == "end_turn"`
options.B: Checking for the presence of assistant text content as a completion indicator
options.C: Continuing the loop while `stop_reason == "tool_use"`
options.D: Feeding tool results back into conversation history between iterations

questions.rationale: Checking for the mere presence of assistant text is unreliable — Claude can produce text alongside a tool call. `stop_reason` is the structured, purpose-built signal; text-presence checks are a known anti-pattern.

questions.question: A coordinator decomposes "impact of remote work on urban economies" into subtasks covering only office real estate and commuting patterns, missing retail, housing, and local tax revenue. What's the root cause and fix?

options.A: The subagents under-researched their assigned subtopics — expand their search queries
options.B: The coordinator's initial decomposition was too narrow — it should cover the topic's full breadth before delegating
options.C: The synthesis agent should have caught the gap and requested more data
options.D: A larger language model would have produced better subagent results

questions.rationale: This is the same failure pattern as narrow topic decomposition seen elsewhere: subagents did their assigned jobs correctly, but the coordinator's initial breakdown didn't cover all relevant domains of the topic in the first place.

questions.question: What are the two `stop_reason` values most relevant to controlling an agentic loop?

options.A: "tool_use" and "end_turn"
options.B: "success" and "failure"
options.C: "continue" and "stop"
options.D: "pending" and "complete"

questions.rationale: These are the two structured signals the API returns: "tool_use" means continue the loop and execute the requested tool; "end_turn" means the model has finished.

questions.question: What is the defining feature of model-driven decision-making in an agentic system, as opposed to a pre-configured decision tree?

options.A: Claude reasons about which tool to call next based on context, rather than following a fixed pre-scripted sequence
options.B: The system never calls the same tool twice
options.C: All decisions are made by a separate classifier model
options.D: The agent requires human approval before every tool call

questions.rationale: Model-driven decision-making means Claude itself reasons about the next action from context, contrasted with rigid, pre-configured tool sequences or decision trees.

questions.question: In coordinator-subagent architectures, do subagents automatically inherit the coordinator's conversation history?

options.A: No — subagents operate with isolated context and must be given relevant information explicitly
options.B: Yes, automatically and completely
options.C: Only the first message is inherited
options.D: Only if `fork_session` is used

questions.rationale: Subagents do not automatically inherit context; any information they need must be explicitly included in the prompt when they're spawned.

questions.question: What tool is used to spawn a subagent in the Claude Agent SDK?

options.A: The `Task` tool
options.B: The `Spawn` tool
options.C: The `Delegate` tool
options.D: The `Fork` tool

questions.rationale: The `Task` tool is the mechanism for spawning subagents; a coordinator's `allowedTools` must include "Task" to use it.

questions.question: What is `fork_session` used for?

options.A: Creating independent branches from a shared analysis baseline to explore divergent approaches
options.B: Permanently deleting a session's history
options.C: Merging two separate sessions into one
options.D: Exporting a session transcript to a file

questions.rationale: `fork_session` lets you branch off a shared baseline to explore multiple approaches independently, without one exploration affecting the other.

questions.question: What CLI mechanism lets you continue a specific prior conversation by name?

options.A: `--resume <session-name>`
options.B: `--continue <session-name>`
options.C: `--load <session-name>`
options.D: `--reopen <session-name>`

questions.rationale: `--resume <session-name>` continues a specific named prior conversation.

questions.question: Why is setting an arbitrary iteration cap considered an anti-pattern as the *primary* loop-termination mechanism?

options.A: It doesn't reflect whether the task has actually finished, and can cut off legitimate work or mask runaway loops
options.B: It's not supported by the Claude API at all
options.C: It forces the agent to always use the maximum number of tool calls
options.D: It requires a separate classifier model to configure

questions.rationale: An iteration cap is a safety net at best, not a substitute for a real completion signal like `stop_reason` — relying on it primarily means stopping for the wrong reason.

questions.question: What's the difference between prompt chaining and dynamic task decomposition?

options.A: Prompt chaining uses a fixed sequence of steps; dynamic decomposition generates subtasks adaptively based on what's discovered
options.B: They are two names for the same technique
options.C: Prompt chaining only works with subagents, dynamic decomposition only works with a single agent
options.D: Dynamic decomposition is always faster than prompt chaining

questions.rationale: Prompt chaining is best for predictable, multi-aspect tasks with known steps; dynamic decomposition suits open-ended tasks where subtasks depend on what's found along the way.

questions.question: What should a structured handoff to a human agent typically include?

options.A: Customer details, root cause analysis, and a recommended action
options.B: Only the customer's original message
options.C: The full internal tool-call log with no summary
options.D: Nothing, since the human should investigate independently

questions.rationale: Since the receiving human often lacks transcript access, a structured summary lets them act quickly on the case.

questions.question: What is a `PostToolUse` hook typically used for?

options.A: Intercepting and transforming tool results before the model processes them
options.B: Blocking a user from sending a new message
options.C: Changing the system prompt after every tool call
options.D: Logging billing information for the API account

questions.rationale: `PostToolUse` hooks intercept tool results for transformation (e.g., normalizing inconsistent data formats) before the model reasons over them.

questions.question: What is the primary mechanism an LLM uses to decide which tool to call?

options.A: The tool's description
options.B: The tool's internal source code
options.C: The order tools are listed in
options.D: The tool's function name length

questions.rationale: Tool descriptions are the primary signal models use for tool selection; minimal or ambiguous descriptions lead to unreliable selection among similar tools.

questions.question: What does the MCP `isError` flag communicate?

options.A: That a tool call failed, allowing the agent to react appropriately
options.B: That the tool is deprecated and should not be used again
options.C: That the user made an invalid request
options.D: That the MCP server is offline

questions.rationale: The `isError` flag is the pattern for communicating tool failures back to the agent so it can decide how to proceed.

questions.question: Where should a shared, team-wide MCP server be configured so credentials aren't committed to version control?

options.A: Project-scoped `.mcp.json`, using environment variable expansion (e.g. `${GITHUB_TOKEN}`)
options.B: Hardcoded directly into the tool's source file
options.C: User-scoped `~/.claude.json` only
options.D: A shared spreadsheet distributed to the team

questions.rationale: Project-scoped `.mcp.json` with environment variable expansion allows shared configuration without committing secrets to version control.

questions.question: What's a key risk of giving an agent access to too many tools (e.g. 18 instead of 4-5)?

options.A: Tool selection reliability degrades as decision complexity increases
options.B: The API automatically rejects requests with more than 10 tools
options.C: Tool descriptions become mandatory only above a certain tool count
options.D: Latency increases, but selection accuracy is unaffected

questions.rationale: Too many available tools — especially outside an agent's specialization — increases the chance of misuse and unreliable tool selection.

questions.question: What does `tool_choice: "any"` guarantee, as opposed to `"auto"`?

options.A: The model must call some tool, though it can choose which one
options.B: The model must call one specific named tool
options.C: The model may return plain text instead of calling a tool
options.D: The model will call every available tool in sequence

questions.rationale: `"any"` forces the model to call a tool (but lets it pick which), whereas `"auto"` allows the model to return text instead, and forced selection names one specific tool.

questions.question: MCP resources are best used for:

options.A: Exposing content catalogs (e.g. schemas, doc hierarchies) to reduce exploratory tool calls
options.B: Executing actions that change state in a backend system
options.C: Replacing the need for tool descriptions
options.D: Storing conversation history between sessions

questions.rationale: Resources expose content catalogs for visibility, while tools are for taking actions — conflating the two undercuts the point of resources.

questions.question: Which built-in tool is best suited to searching file *contents* for a specific pattern (like a function name)?

options.A: Grep
options.B: Glob
options.C: Read
options.D: Edit

questions.rationale: Grep searches file contents for patterns; Glob matches file paths/names, not content.

questions.question: When `Edit` fails because the target text isn't unique in a file, what's the recommended fallback?

options.A: Use `Read` to load the full file, then `Write` the modified version
options.B: Retry `Edit` with the exact same arguments
options.C: Switch to `Bash` to run a sed command instead
options.D: Delete and recreate the file from scratch

questions.rationale: Read + Write is the standard fallback for reliable modification when Edit's unique-text-match requirement can't be satisfied.

questions.question: Why might overlapping or ambiguous tool descriptions (e.g. `analyze_content` vs `analyze_document`) cause problems?

options.A: They cause the agent to misroute requests between similarly-described tools
options.B: They cause the MCP server to crash on startup
options.C: They are automatically merged into a single tool by the SDK
options.D: They only matter if `tool_choice` is set to "auto"

questions.rationale: Near-identical descriptions give the model insufficient signal to differentiate tools, leading to misrouting regardless of `tool_choice` setting.

questions.question: What's the difference between `.mcp.json` and `~/.claude.json` for MCP server configuration?

options.A: `.mcp.json` is project-scoped and shared via version control; `~/.claude.json` is user-scoped and personal
options.B: They are interchangeable and always produce identical behavior
options.C: `~/.claude.json` is only for production servers, `.mcp.json` only for testing
options.D: `.mcp.json` cannot use environment variables

questions.rationale: Project-scoped `.mcp.json` is for shared team tooling; user-scoped `~/.claude.json` is for personal or experimental servers.

questions.question: What is the correct order of specificity in the CLAUDE.md configuration hierarchy?

options.A: User-level → project-level → directory-level
options.B: Directory-level → user-level → project-level
options.C: There is no hierarchy; all CLAUDE.md files are equivalent
options.D: Project-level always overrides directory-level

questions.rationale: CLAUDE.md configuration flows from broad (user-level, personal) to project-level (shared via version control) to directory-level (most specific).

questions.question: Why might a new team member fail to receive expected coding conventions even though the project's CLAUDE.md looks correct?

options.A: The conventions were placed in `~/.claude/CLAUDE.md` (user-level), which isn't shared via version control
options.B: CLAUDE.md files are cached and take 24 hours to propagate
options.C: Only the project owner's CLAUDE.md is ever loaded
options.D: New team members must manually copy CLAUDE.md into their home directory

questions.rationale: User-level CLAUDE.md settings apply only to that individual user and are never shared via version control — a common cause of "it works for me but not my teammate."

questions.question: What does the `@import` syntax in CLAUDE.md allow?

options.A: Referencing external files to keep CLAUDE.md modular
options.B: Importing a different AI model for a specific task
options.C: Pulling in a teammate's personal settings automatically
options.D: Triggering a CI/CD pipeline run

questions.rationale: `@import` references external files so CLAUDE.md doesn't have to be one large monolithic file.

questions.question: What's the advantage of `.claude/rules/` files with glob-pattern frontmatter over directory-level CLAUDE.md files?

options.A: They apply conventions to files by type regardless of where those files live in the directory tree
options.B: They load faster than CLAUDE.md files
options.C: They replace the need for a project-level CLAUDE.md entirely
options.D: They only work for test files

questions.rationale: Glob-pattern rules (e.g. `**/*.test.tsx`) apply based on file type/pattern rather than directory location, which matters when relevant files are scattered throughout a codebase.

questions.question: Where should a custom slash command live so it's shared with the whole team via version control?

options.A: `.claude/commands/` in the project repository
options.B: `~/.claude/commands/` in each developer's home directory
options.C: Inside the root CLAUDE.md file
options.D: A `.claude/config.json` commands array

questions.rationale: `.claude/commands/` is version-controlled and project-scoped; `~/.claude/commands/` is personal and not shared.

questions.question: What does the `context: fork` frontmatter option do for a skill?

options.A: Runs the skill in an isolated sub-agent context so its output doesn't pollute the main conversation
options.B: Forks the entire git repository automatically
options.C: Duplicates the skill for every team member
options.D: Forces the skill to run twice for verification

questions.rationale: `context: fork` isolates verbose or exploratory skill output from the main session's context.

questions.question: When is plan mode most appropriate, compared to direct execution?

options.A: For complex tasks with architectural implications, multiple valid approaches, or large-scale multi-file changes
options.B: For any single-line bug fix
options.C: Only when working with MCP servers
options.D: Whenever `stop_reason` is "tool_use"

questions.rationale: Plan mode is designed for exploration and design before committing to complex, high-stakes changes; simple well-scoped changes are better handled with direct execution.

questions.question: What does the `/memory` command help you do?

options.A: Verify which memory (CLAUDE.md) files are currently loaded, to diagnose inconsistent behavior
options.B: Permanently erase all session history
options.C: Switch between different Claude models mid-session
options.D: Generate a summary of the current git diff

questions.rationale: `/memory` shows which memory files are loaded, which helps diagnose why behavior might differ across sessions or team members.

questions.question: What CLI flag runs Claude Code in non-interactive mode, suitable for CI/CD pipelines?

options.A: `-p` (or `--print`)
options.B: `--headless`
options.C: `--batch`

questions.rationale: `-p`/`--print` processes the prompt and exits without waiting for interactive input — the documented approach for automated pipelines.

questions.question: What do `--output-format json` and `--json-schema` enable in a CI context?

options.A: Machine-parseable, structured output that can be posted as automated PR comments
options.B: Faster execution time for large codebases
options.C: Automatic retries on failure
options.D: Skipping the need for a CLAUDE.md file

questions.rationale: These flags enforce structured, schema-compliant output so CI tooling can reliably parse and act on Claude Code's findings.

questions.question: What's the most reliable way to guarantee schema-compliant structured output from Claude?

options.A: `tool_use` with a JSON schema as the tool's input parameters
options.B: Asking nicely in the system prompt for valid JSON
options.C: Post-processing free-text output with regular expressions
options.D: Increasing `max_tokens`

questions.rationale: Tool use with JSON schemas eliminates JSON syntax errors, unlike relying on the model to freely produce well-formed JSON in text.

questions.question: Does enforcing a strict JSON schema via tool use prevent semantic errors (e.g. line items that don't sum to the stated total)?

options.A: No — it eliminates syntax errors but not semantic/logical errors
options.B: Yes, schemas fully guarantee semantic correctness
options.C: Only if `tool_choice` is set to "auto"
options.D: Only for numeric fields

questions.rationale: Schema enforcement guarantees structural validity, not semantic correctness — separate validation is needed to catch things like totals that don't add up.

questions.question: Why should extraction schema fields be marked nullable rather than required when the source document may not contain that information?

options.A: To prevent the model from fabricating values just to satisfy a required field
options.B: Because JSON schemas don't support optional fields
options.C: To make the schema smaller and faster to validate
options.D: Because nullable fields are always faster to extract

questions.rationale: Forcing a required field when the source doesn't express that information invites the model to fabricate a plausible-looking but invented value.

questions.question: What is the most effective technique for achieving consistently formatted output when detailed prose instructions alone produce inconsistent results?

options.A: Few-shot examples
options.B: Increasing the temperature setting
options.C: Adding more adjectives to the instructions
options.D: Splitting the prompt into more system messages

questions.rationale: Few-shot examples demonstrate the desired output format and handling of ambiguous cases more reliably than prose instructions alone.

questions.question: What's a key limitation of the Message Batches API?

options.A: No guaranteed latency SLA and no multi-turn tool calling within a single request
options.B: It cannot be used for more than 10 requests at a time
options.C: It costs more than synchronous API calls
options.D: It only supports single-field JSON schemas

questions.rationale: Batches offer cost savings but trade off guaranteed latency and don't support multi-turn tool calling mid-request — making them unsuitable for blocking, time-sensitive workflows.

questions.question: What field is used to correlate a Message Batches API request with its corresponding response?

options.A: `custom_id`
options.B: `request_hash`
options.C: `batch_key`
options.D: `trace_id`

questions.rationale: `custom_id` fields let you match each submitted request to its response, especially useful when resubmitting only failed items.

questions.question: Why do vague instructions like "be conservative" or "only report high-confidence findings" often fail to reduce false positives?

options.A: They don't provide the explicit, specific criteria needed for the model to reliably distinguish real issues from false ones
options.B: They cause the model to stop producing output entirely
options.C: They only work when combined with a higher temperature
options.D: They are not supported by the API

questions.rationale: Specific categorical criteria are far more effective than general instructions to "be careful," which give the model no concrete basis for the judgment call.

questions.question: When a validation-retry loop fails repeatedly on a field, what should you check before retrying again?

options.A: Whether the information is actually present in the source document at all — retries won't help if it's genuinely absent
options.B: Whether `max_tokens` is set high enough
options.C: Whether the schema has too many required fields
options.D: Whether the retry request used the same temperature as the original

questions.rationale: Retries are effective for format/structural errors, but ineffective when the required information simply isn't present in the source — no amount of retrying recovers data that was never there.

questions.question: Why is a second, independent Claude instance often more effective at reviewing generated code than asking the same instance to self-review?

options.A: The generating instance retains reasoning context from creating the code, making it less likely to question its own decisions
options.B: A second instance always uses a larger context window
options.C: Self-review is not technically possible with the API
options.D: Independent instances are cheaper to run

questions.rationale: Self-review within the same session inherits the generator's own reasoning and blind spots; an independent instance without that context can catch issues more objectively.

questions.question: What's the purpose of forced tool selection (`tool_choice: {"type": "tool", "name": "..."}`)?

options.A: To guarantee a specific named tool is called, e.g. to enforce a required first step like metadata extraction
options.B: To prevent the model from calling any tool at all
options.C: To let the model choose freely among all available tools
options.D: To disable JSON schema validation for that call

questions.rationale: Forced selection ensures one specific tool runs, useful when a particular step (like extracting metadata first) must happen before others.

questions.question: What is the "lost in the middle" effect?

options.A: Models reliably process information at the beginning and end of long inputs but may miss details from middle sections
options.B: Conversations lose their system prompt after 10 turns
options.C: Tool results disappear from context after being used once
options.D: Claude forgets the user's name partway through a session

questions.rationale: This describes a known pattern where information placed in the middle of long inputs is more likely to be underweighted or missed compared to the start or end.

questions.question: What's a risk of progressive summarization in long conversations?

options.A: Specific numerical values, dates, and stated expectations can get condensed into vague, lossy summaries
options.B: It always increases token usage instead of reducing it
options.C: It can only be applied once per session
options.D: It automatically deletes the system prompt

questions.rationale: Summarization that isn't careful about preserving concrete facts (amounts, dates, exact expectations) risks losing information that later reasoning depends on.

questions.question: When should an agent escalate to a human, according to reliable escalation design?

options.A: On explicit customer request, when policy is silent/ambiguous on the situation, or when no meaningful progress can be made
options.B: Whenever the conversation exceeds 5 turns
options.C: Whenever sentiment analysis detects any negative tone
options.D: Only when the agent's self-reported confidence drops below a fixed number

questions.rationale: Sentiment-based and self-reported-confidence triggers are both unreliable proxies for actual complexity; explicit request, policy gaps, and genuine stuckness are the reliable triggers.

questions.question: What should structured error context passed to a coordinator include, beyond a simple failure status?

options.A: Failure type, what was attempted, any partial results, and possible alternative approaches
options.B: Just a boolean indicating success or failure
options.C: The full raw exception stack trace and nothing else
options.D: A generic "unavailable" message to keep payloads small

questions.rationale: Rich structured error context lets the coordinator make an informed recovery decision rather than guessing blindly from a generic status.

questions.question: Why is aggregate accuracy (e.g. "97% overall") potentially misleading for an extraction system?

options.A: It can mask poor performance on specific document types or fields that are underrepresented in the aggregate
options.B: Aggregate accuracy is always inflated by at least 10%
options.C: It only applies to numeric fields
options.D: It cannot be measured for extraction tasks at all

questions.rationale: A high overall number can hide segments (particular document types or fields) where accuracy is actually much worse — stratified analysis is needed to catch this.

questions.question: What is stratified random sampling used for in this context?

options.A: Measuring error rates within high-confidence extractions and catching novel error patterns that aggregate metrics might hide
options.B: Randomly selecting which MCP server to call
options.C: Choosing which subagent should run first
options.D: Deciding the batch size for the Message Batches API

questions.rationale: Stratified sampling across document types/fields helps verify that even "high-confidence" extractions are actually accurate, rather than trusting the aggregate number blindly.

questions.question: Why should information provenance (claim-source mappings) be explicitly preserved during multi-source synthesis?

options.A: Summarization steps can otherwise lose track of which finding came from which source
options.B: It's required by the Claude API for all tool calls
options.C: It only matters for numeric data, not qualitative findings
options.D: It automatically resolves conflicting data between sources
